analysis.title: $1 Trillion A Day, $11 Million Deep: Goldman Finds Record Volumes Masking A Market That's "Thinnest Exactly When It's Needed Most"
key_insights: Goldman S&T (Jason Klein) Liquidity snapshot: YTD US equity volumes average a record 19B shares / $1T a day. Volumes are up 10% y/y through 3Q, but top-of-book liquidity is flat and the trading environment remains fragile.

Average daily executed value in US equities doubled since 2023, from $511B to $1.041T. S&P top-of-book liquidity (dollar value of bids and offers at the best price) fell 21% over the same period, from $14M to $11M.

ZeroHedge's calculation of depth per $1B traded: about $162K in 2017, about $12K in 2022 (bear market, fastest Fed hiking cycle in four decades), roughly $11K in 2026. That is the thinnest on record, below the 2022 trough and down 93% from 2017, with the S&P near record highs.

June 2026 had the two busiest volume days ever: 33B shares on June 18 (quad-witching pulled forward by Juneteenth, the morning after the Fed's hawkish dot-plot surprise from Warsh on Jun 17) and 32B on June 26 (Russell reconstitution). Nasdaq's closing cross on June 26 executed a record $334B vs $102B a year earlier.

June top-of-book liquidity fell 33% vs May, from $12M to $8M, even as monthly average volume hit a 2026 high of 22.8B shares. The day before the Fed, S&P top of book was $2.69M, down 68% vs its 20-day average.
Depth recovered to a YTD high of $15M in September on a monthly average basis. ZeroHedge notes the average hides air pockets, citing e-mini top-of-book liquidity at 0 on September 16, 2026.
In share terms, top-of-book depth is down 76% since 2017, from $45M to $11M, while daily share volume nearly tripled from 6.5B to 18.7B. Depth has been stable at about $11M for the past two years.

ZeroHedge attributes the volume to wrappers and derivatives (0DTE options, levered ETFs, macro hedging products). It argues this is churn, hedging and leverage flow that consumes liquidity rather than provides it.

Klein's key point: despite the higher-volume regime, top-of-book depth still evaporates in stressed tapes, 'thinnest exactly when it's needed most.' Each volume spike pairs with a depth collapse. The post-Liberation Day crash was the extreme case, with ES top of book at $1MM on April 7, 2025.

JPMorgan's Delta-One desk reported that during last week's global bond rout, US bond futures market depth was about 3-4 standard deviations below average (5-6 in EMEA). Dip-buyers still produced the largest weekly net buying of US bond futures in the bank's 5-year history.
Today's 30Y Treasury auction priced at the highest yield since August 2000. ZeroHedge ties the relentless bond selling to Japanese repatriation, with France seen as next.

Today's tape: the FT reported OpenAI's annualized revenue is roughly $20B below what had been signaled to investors, and the Nasdaq fell more than 1% with the AI basket sharply lower. Goldman's Mid-Day Color described a defensive tilt on Middle East escalation fears, with the Russell 2000 underperforming for a fifth straight session and breaking below its 200-day moving average. Long-onlys and hedge funds skewed to sell, and desk activity was 4 out of 10.

ZeroHedge's view (not Goldman's): the market is crowded rather than liquid, and the odds favor the next air pocket arriving sooner rather than later. A 1% move could become a 3% move if depth disappears.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Weak demand and ongoing global bond selling. Thin futures depth raises the risk of outsized moves in rates and spillover into equities.
Record volume, but not matched by resting liquidity.

risk_factors: Thin top-of-book depth can turn a 1% move into a 3% move when selling starts

E-mini top-of-book liquidity was 0 on September 16, 2026, and under $2M on June 26 (Russell reconstitution), per ZeroHedge.
Hedge funds and long-onlys skewed to sell in today's session. The Russell 2000 underperformed for a fifth straight session and broke below its 200-day moving average.

Earlier 2026 Goldman flow commentary cited by ZeroHedge: CTAs were sellers in every scenario as liquidity evaporated (Gail Hafif, Jun 10), and Brian Garrett found 4.7x more short covering than long buying.
Single-stock liquidity is shrinking as activity moves into ETFs, 0DTE options and levered ETFs. ETFs were 39% of the tape in March.
